prompt: Which statement about a market order is correct?

options.text: A market order always fills at the best price.
A market order can fill at several prices, so its average fill can be worse than the best price shown.
A market order waits until the price reaches the best price.
A market order fills only at the closing price.

explanations.a: A large market order takes shares at more than one price when the best level is thin.
explanations.c: A market order does not wait. It takes what is offered now.
explanations.d: A market order is not tied to the close. It fills at the prices available when it is placed.

prompt: Hypothetical. The best ask is Rs 250.00 for 100 shares and the next ask is Rs 250.50 for 100 shares. What is the average fill for a market buy of 200 shares, in rupees per share?
Hypothetical. With the same book, a market buy of 150 shares is filled. What is the slippage against the best ask, in rupees?
solution: First 100 shares at Rs 250.00 = Rs 25,000. Next 50 shares at Rs 250.50 = Rs 12,525. Total = Rs 37,525. Shares at the best ask = 150 x Rs 250.00 = Rs 37,500. Slippage = 37,525 - 37,500 = Rs 25. Checked again: 50 shares x Rs 0.50 above the best ask = Rs 25.

prompt: Which statement about the opening auction is correct?

options.text: The opening price is the first trade of the day, with no orders collected first.
The opening auction collects orders first, then sets one price from them.
The opening auction sets a different price for each order.
An auction works the same as continuous trading, with a new price on each trade.

explanations.a: The opening auction collects orders before it sets a price. The first trade is not simply the first order.
explanations.c: An auction sets one price for the auction. It does not set a price for each order.
explanations.d: In an auction, orders are collected before a single price is set. Continuous trading works differently.

prompt: A limit buy order is at Rs 250.00. The price touches Rs 250.00. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The order fills at once, because the price reached it.
The order may not fill, because orders ahead of it in the queue may take the shares first.
The order fills at Rs 249.00, which is the lower price.
The order is cancelled automatically when the price touches it.

explanations.a: A touch does not guarantee a fill. Orders ahead of yours may take the shares.
explanations.c: A limit buy fills at its limit or better, not at a lower price that was never offered.
explanations.d: A touch does not cancel the order. It waits in the queue.

prompt: Hypothetical. A thin stock has a wide spread at the open. A paper log records every market order at the best ask. What is the main risk to the log's accuracy?

options.text: The log is accurate, since the best ask is the price.
The log hides slippage and queue effects, so paper results can look better than real ones.
The log will show too many shares.
Only the closing price matters for the log.

explanations.a: The best ask is only the first price. A thin book can fill the rest at higher prices.
explanations.c: The share count is not the problem. The price used for each fill is.
explanations.d: The open and the trading during the day also produce fills. The closing price does not fix this.

prompt: Spot the mistake: "My paper log records each market buy at the best ask shown, so my paper results match what I would get." Which part is wrong?

options.text: My paper log: a paper log is a useful habit when its method is honest.
records each market buy at the best ask shown
The word paper: paper logs are never useful.
Nothing. The statement is correct.

explanations.a: A paper log is useful. The problem is the price method it uses.
explanations.c: Paper logs are useful when they are honest about fills. This word is not the mistake.
explanations.d: The statement is wrong. Recording only the best ask ignores fills at higher prices in a thin book.
